intro: Looking for a lease extension conveyancer near you usually means your lease is getting shorter and you want to understand your options before it affects your home. Perhaps you're thinking of selling, remortgaging, or you've been told a short lease could hold things up. A local conveyancer who deals with lease extensions can explain the statutory route and how a valuer fits into the process.
need_heading: What people searching for a lease extension conveyancer usually need
need_lead: Most people who search for a lease extension conveyancer are weighing up whether to extend, when to start, and who should handle the legal side.
needs: You've owned your flat for a while and the lease is now short enough that a lender or buyer has raised concerns about it.
You want to know whether you qualify for a statutory lease extension and what the procedure involves before you commit.
You're planning to sell and want the lease extended so your flat is easier to market and mortgage.
You've received an informal quote from your freeholder but want independent legal help to check the terms.
You need a conveyancer who can work alongside a valuer and liaise with your freeholder or their solicitor.
context_heading: Understanding the statutory lease extension route
context: Extending a lease under statutory rights follows a set procedure, and a specialist conveyancer usually works alongside a valuer to establish the premium. Short leases can affect both the value of your home and your ability to get a mortgage, so timing matters.

Conveyancing in England and Wales is a reserved legal activity, carried out by solicitors regulated by the SRA or licensed conveyancers regulated by the Council for Licensed Conveyancers. Both must hold professional indemnity insurance and follow strict rules on handling client money. If your lender has a panel, check the firm is on it before you instruct them, as many lenders only work with conveyancers on their panel.

faqs.q: Do I need a valuer as well as a conveyancer?
faqs.a: Yes, usually. A lease extension specialist handles the legal procedure, while a valuer assesses the premium. The two work together, so it helps to ask your conveyancer how they coordinate with a valuer.

faqs.q: What is a statutory lease extension?
faqs.a: It's a route under the law that lets qualifying leaseholders extend their lease in a set way, rather than negotiating informally with the freeholder. A conveyancer can explain whether you qualify and what the process involves.

faqs.q: Will a short lease affect my mortgage?
faqs.a: It can. Many lenders are cautious about short leases, and a short lease can also affect the value of your home. Extending the lease can help, so it's worth speaking to a conveyancer early.

faqs.q: How do I check a conveyancer is properly regulated?
faqs.a: Solicitors are regulated by the SRA and licensed conveyancers by the Council for Licensed Conveyancers. Both must hold professional indemnity insurance, so ask which regulator they fall under before you instruct them.

extra_heading: Choosing a local lease extension conveyancer
extra: Searching for a lease extension conveyancer near you suggests you'd rather deal with someone you could meet or call locally, and that's a reasonable instinct for a process that can run alongside your freeholder and a valuer. Being nearby isn't essential in itself, though, because much of the work is done in writing and over the phone. What matters more is that the person handling your claim does lease extension work regularly and can explain each stage clearly as it unfolds.

When you compare the options iComply introduces you to, ask each one directly about their experience of statutory lease extension claims rather than leasehold work in general. Ask who will actually handle your file day to day, how they will keep you informed, and how they coordinate with your valuer on the premium. Because quotes are on application, ask what the quote covers and whether anything is likely to be charged separately, so you can weigh up the options fairly.

It also helps to be clear about where you are in the process before you speak to anyone. If you've already served notice or had terms back from your freeholder, say so, as it changes what the conveyancer needs to do next. If you're starting from scratch, they can talk you through the statutory route and what a valuer will need from you. Either way, a short first conversation usually tells you whether the fit feels right.

extra_faqs.q: Does my lease extension conveyancer need to be local to me or to the property?
extra_faqs.a: Not strictly. Lease extension work is largely handled in writing and by phone, so a conveyancer further away can act for you perfectly well. What matters most is that they regularly handle statutory lease extensions and that you can reach them easily when you need to.

extra_faqs.q: Can I use my existing conveyancer for a lease extension?
extra_faqs.a: You can ask them, but it's worth checking whether they do lease extension work routinely, as it's a distinct area with its own procedure. If they don't, they may suggest you instruct someone who does. Either way, ask about their experience before you decide.

extra_faqs.q: What if my freeholder is hard to reach or won't engage?
extra_faqs.a: The statutory route sets out steps that must be followed, and a conveyancer can explain what happens when a freeholder doesn't respond or disputes the claim. It's worth raising this early so you understand the options. Ask how they would handle it before you instruct them.
